jobs.name: Computer Science 144 Head Project Demi
jobs.brief: Developing the project, its reference implementation, the specification, and test script / suite for first-year students at Stellenbosch University.

points.text: At the end of 2025, I began working with Prof. Lynette van Zijl and later Prof. van der Merwe in developing the Computer Science 144 semester project that first-year Computer Science students will receive during the module in their second semester.

The students will be required to implement a Python program, the nature thereof I will share here when I am permitted. I was tasked with designing a project suitable for the skill level of first-years that focused on Object-Oriented Programming principles. I had to design a unique project that students could not simply download a solution for.

As part of this process, I developed a full implementation of the project, called the Oracle, which acted as the true, 'correct' solution of the project. The Oracle was used to develop the test suite, so that the outputs would exactly match that of what the program was meant to generate.

I also wrote a marking script that would automatically mark all student submissions, as the students' code was specified to behave deterministically. This script will mark student submissions by running their solution through test suites applicable to the given submission, and give them a mark determined by a weighted sum of their pass rate in each test-case category.
This marking script also acts as a tool that students can use to check their own code before submission, with the incomplete test-suite.
I wrote the student specification for the project in LaTeX, as required by the professors, that strictly detailed what the students were to implement.

In the second semester of 2026, I will be tasked with running the project, which will entail running Q&A sessions, answering student query emails, resolving issues, and handling the project-marking (using the marking script) on a weekly basis.

Overall, this project has given me some great Software Engineering practice, as I've learned to work with clients (the professors), write a formal specification, spend a large amount of time on correctness testing (both for the Oracle and the students' implementation), and conform to time constraints. It has also been the most significant engineering project that I have done with high stakes that are not just about University marks.
I am looking forward to the latter half of the year, where I will have the honour of running this project for a couple hundred students.

projects_personal.name: Little Explorers Website [Frontend]
projects_personal.brief: Informational website for Little Explorers for prospective clients to decide if they wish to send their child to the centre.

points.text: My mother owns and runs a preschool and aftercare from home called "Little Explorers Aftercare and Preschool." For most of its lifetime, it's had a simple website written in PHP by my father. It was a good website, but had a few issues. Firstly, the information was completely outdated, as the services offered by Little Explorers have changed over the years. Its style is also dated. The largest issue was a lack of adaptivity, meaning that the website looked terrible on a mobile screen.

After my webdev course in 3rd year, I proposed to my family that I design a new website to resolve these issues, as my father didn't have the modern-day skills to perform such a task. My mother is a very busy woman, so my father incrementally elicited requirements from her and put it all in basic HTML in the old website's PHP structure.

In early February, I ported all the existing code from PHP to TypeScript with React (Using some help from ChatGPT to speed things up), then worked on overhauling the CSS, adding some icons, using React Router for navigation, and most importantly, making the website adaptive.
After all of this, I used FTP to upload the built website via the absolutehosting service that my dad has been using to keep the website live.
Below the links, I have some comparison pictures between the old website and the new website.
Note, the images above don't document all changes, just some examples.

In the future, should I find the time, I would also like to implement a backend for Little Explorers that will allow users of the website to send enquiries and see a display of recent posts from the Little Explorers Instagram and Facebook accounts, and to create a database that could automate a lot of the admin my mother does manually to make her life easier.
If you have a child in the Durbanville area in need of a preschool or aftercare, Little Explorers would love to have you.

projects_university.name: LEGO Instructions Animation
projects_university.brief: My honours project. A tool that takes PDF LEGO instructions and converts them to live, steppable 3D animations.

points.text: I am currently working on my honours project under the supervision of Lynette van Zijl. The goal of the project is to take official LEGO instructions and do some magic to turn those instructions into 3D animations.

The way this has been achieved is via an intermediate language of my own design, called LLL. This language allows users to write code that describes operations over LEGO sets, like spawning parts, creating partial builds, duplicating partial builds, attaching parts, and more. This provides a user-friendly text-based way of describing instructions in a way that can be meaningfully interpreted by a graphics engine.

points.caption: An example of the LLL language.

points.text: This language gets translated down to an intermediate representation called the LAL via a translator built in C#. The LAL is parsed into a dictionary in the Godot game engine, where GDScript processes it and produces the live animation.

points.caption: A video of an animation produced by the program.

points.text: Note that this project isn't complete, as it's my year project for 2026. In June, I will be working on tooling to convert official LEGO instructions to LLL via PDF parsing and computer vision. I will share more details on this as I go.

hackathons.name: SUDS Hackathon Winners
hackathons.brief: Winners of the Stellenbosch Developer's Society 2025 Hackathon.

points.text: Dylan Swarts and I participated against 7 other teams in the SUDS Hackathon of 2025. The theme was to build something that would improve student life. Swarts and I (as a team called "Dylan Squared" since we are both called Dylan) developed a full-stack system called " Maroonut", a digitized version of the Stellenbosch University's Faculty yearbook. We built this system over a 38-hour period from Friday, 3 October at 20:00 (Right after writing a 3rd year maths exam) to Sunday, 5 October at 10:00. The full implementation and detailed README can be found on GitHub via the link below.

points.name: Check out the website of my teammate, Dylan Swarts

points.caption: When you first arrive at maroonut, you will land on the home page, detailing the purpose and functionality of the service.

points.text: Maroonut uses React Router, so you can bookmark any page and share links to certain modules directly.

points.caption: You can log in to your own account, which allows you to view modules, post reviews on modules you've already completed, and even advertise yourself as a tutor for specific modules.

points.text: Note that user authentication was not fully implemented as it was not the focus during our short timeframe, but future versions would likely authenticate via Stellenbosch's existing database.

points.caption: Once logged in, you can view all modules and even search for modules based on search terms to find what you're looking for.

Every module has a dedicated page with the module's framework, lecture and tutorial hours, and the module's pre- and corequisites, which also act as buttons to direct you to those modules. The module rating is based off of an average of all reviewers' ratings of the module.

Scrolling further down, you can view reviews for the module by people who have taken it in the past. This allows you to gauge more about the module than a module framework allows, as you hear students' real-world experience with the module to better advise you. If you've passed a module, you can give your own review on it, and rate it by clicking on the stars. Users can also gift and revoke 'acorns' to and from the review. Reviews are sorted in descending order by acorns so that the best reviews stay at the top.
You can also see users who are tutoring for the module, showing a brief description of each tutor's service and their rate, as well as buttons to contact them via email and visit their profiles.
On a user's profile page, you can see how many acorns they've been gifted over reviews, modules taken and their outcomes, and modules they've reviewed or are tutoring for.
